can you update @src/distance.jl so it adds a diffusion distance metric to check the probability that a random walk starting at one node would get to another node after t steps, according to the algorithm below?

Setup

Let G = (U ∪ V, E) be bipartite with biadjacency matrix B ∈ ℝ^{|U|×|V|} (weighted or 0/1). The full adjacency matrix is

A = [[0, B], [Bᵀ, 0]], D = diag(A·1), P = D⁻¹A.

P is the one-step transition matrix of a random walk. The diffusion distance at time t between vertices i, j is

D_t(i, j)² = Σ_k (P^t_{ik} − P^t_{jk})² / π_k, where π_k = d_k / vol(G).

The bipartite problem

G is bipartite, so every walk alternates sides. P^t_{ik} = 0 whenever k is on the wrong side for the parity of t. Consequences:

For i ∈ U, j ∈ V, the rows P^t_i and P^t_j have disjoint supports, so D_t(i, j) is large and nearly uninformative for cross-side pairs.
P has eigenvalue −1 (eigenvector +1 on U, −1 on V), so P^t does not converge to π. The walk is periodic.

Two standard fixes:

Lazy walk: P_L = (I + P)/2. Eigenvalues become (1+λ)/2 ∈ [0, 1], so the −1 eigenvalue disappears and P_L^t → 1πᵀ.
Two-step walk, per side: work with P² restricted to U: P_U = D_U⁻¹ B D_V⁻¹ Bᵀ (and P_V analogously). This gives a diffusion distance among same-side vertices only, which is natural if your ε-cohesive core compares vertices within U and within V.
Algorithm (spectral, preferred)

Use the symmetric normalization S = D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}.

Compute S. Eigendecompose S = Σ_k λ_k ψ_k ψ_kᵀ with 1 = λ_1 ≥ λ_2 ≥ … ≥ λ_n ≥ −1. Because G is bipartite, the spectrum is symmetric about 0, and the singular values of D_U^{-1/2} B D_V^{-1/2} equal the nonnegative eigenvalues.
Right eigenvectors of P: φ_k = D^{-1/2} ψ_k.
For the lazy walk, use μ_k = (1+λ_k)/2. For the diffusion map at time t:

Ψ_t(i) = (μ_1^t φ_1(i), μ_2^t φ_2(i), …, μ_n^t φ_n(i)).

Then D_t(i, j) = ‖Ψ_t(i) − Ψ_t(j)‖₂. This is exact when all n eigenpairs are kept, and truncating to the top m eigenpairs gives an approximation with error controlled by μ_{m+1}^t.

Drop k = 1, since φ_1 is constant and contributes nothing to differences.

SVD shortcut. You don’t need the (|U|+|V|)-dimensional eigenproblem. Take the SVD of M = D_U^{-1/2} B D_V^{-1/2} = Σ_k σ_k a_k b_kᵀ. The eigenpairs of S are λ = ±σ_k with ψ = (1/√2)[a_k; ±b_k] (and for σ_1 = 1, ψ_1 ∝ [D_U^{1/2}1; D_V^{1/2}1] normalized). This costs a |U|×|V| SVD and is cheaper for unbalanced sides.

Algorithm (direct, small graphs)
Build P_L = (I + D⁻¹A)/2.
Compute P_L^t by repeated multiplication (or matrix_power).
D_t(i, j)² = Σ_k (P_L^t[i,k] − P_L^t[j,k])² / π_k.

This is O(n³ log t) with dense matrices, so it’s fine for validation but not for large graphs. For sparse graphs, you can instead propagate only the rows you need: x ← x P_L, t times, costing O(t · |E|) per source vertex.
